literal: The empress of Xiaozhao was surnamed Yuan; in deliberating the protocol of respect they did not wish to extend it broadly, and so adopted Shou's opinion.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaozhao's consort was of the Yuan clan; when the court debated the protocol of honoring former rulers, they did not wish to extend it broadly and followed Shou's view.

literal: He was also made concurrent Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent and relieved of Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: He was also appointed concurrent junior tutor of the heir apparent and relieved of palace attendant.

literal: The emperor, because the Book of Wei had not yet been promulgated, ordered Shou to examine it further.
idiomatic: Because the Book of Wei had not yet been issued, the emperor ordered Shou to review it again.

literal: Shou received the order and made many corrections.
idiomatic: Shou obeyed and revised it extensively.

literal: When the order came to promulgate the Book of Wei, Shou held that placing it only in the Secret Archive left outsiders no means to see it; he therefore had one copy sent to the Bing office and one to Ye, and allowed anyone to copy it.
idiomatic: When the throne ordered the Book of Wei circulated, Shou argued that locking it in the secret archive barred the public; he had one copy sent to the Bing secretariat and one to Ye and let anyone copy it.

literal: In the first year of Daning he was given the distinction of opening an office.
idiomatic: In the first year of Daning he was granted an open office.

literal: In the second year of Heqing he was made concurrent Right Vice Director of the Secretariat.
idiomatic: In the second year of Heqing he was made concurrent right vice director of the secretariat.

literal: At that time Emperor Wucheng drank deep all day; court business was entrusted entirely to Palace Attendant Gao Yuanhai.
idiomatic: Emperor Wucheng then drank all day long, leaving court affairs entirely to palace attendant Gao Yuanhai.

literal: Yuanhai was mediocre and unfit for a weighty post; because Shou's talent and fame stirred the age and Director of the Department of State Affairs Bi Yiyun excelled at decisive judgment, they relied on them with earnest trust.
idiomatic: Yuanhai was commonplace and unfit for great responsibility; Shou's talent and fame shook the age, and Bi Yiyun as director of the department of state affairs excelled at cutting through cases—so the emperor leaned on them in earnest.

literal: Shou shrank back and could not correct and save the situation; critics mocked him for it.
idiomatic: Shou shrank from remonstrance and could not set things right; critics jeered at him.

literal: The emperor at Hualin Garden separately raised the Xuanyuan Park, furnished with the beauty of mountains, waters, terraces, and towers; he ordered Shou painted on a loft—such was the esteem in which he was held.
idiomatic: At Hualin the emperor built the separate Xuanyuan Park, stocked with hills, water, terraces, and towers, and ordered Shou painted on a pavilion gallery—such was his favor.

literal: At first, compared with Wen Zisheng and Xing Shao, Shou was somewhat the later arrival; after Shao was dismissed and expelled and Zisheng died in prison for his crime, Shou was greatly employed and stood alone in his time.
idiomatic: Early on Shou had ranked after Wen Zisheng and Xing Shao; once Shao was driven out and Zisheng died in prison for his crimes, Shou rose to sole eminence.

literal: Critics tore one another down; each had his faction.
idiomatic: Rivals slandered one another, each with his own clique.

literal: Whenever Shou spoke he disparaged Xing Shao's writing.
idiomatic: Shou always spoke down Xing Shao's prose.

literal: Shao also said: "In the south Ren Fang's literary style was by nature loose; Wei Shou did not merely imitate—he stole broadly.
idiomatic: Shao also said, "South of the Yangtze, Ren Fang's style was loose by nature; Wei Shou did not just imitate him—he stole wholesale.

literal: " When Shou heard it he said: "He often raids Shen Yue's Collected Works as a thief—what does he mean, saying I stole Ren Fang?
idiomatic: " Hearing this, Shou said, "He is forever burgling the Collected Works of Shen Yue—why accuse me of stealing Ren Fang?

literal: Ren and Shen both enjoyed great renown; Xing and Wei each favored one side.
idiomatic: Ren and Shen both bore great names; Xing and Wei each took a side.

literal: During Wuping, Yellow Gate Gentleman Yan Zhitui put the two lords' opinions to Vice Director Zu Ting; Ting replied: "To see whether Xing and Wei approve or condemn is to know the relative merits of Ren and Shen.
idiomatic: In Wuping, yellow gate gentleman Yan Zhitui asked vice director Zu Ting what the two grandees thought; Ting answered, "Judge Xing and Wei for praise or blame, and you know Ren and Shen's worth.

literal: Shou held that Wen Zisheng never wrote a fu at all, and though Xing had one or two pieces they were not his strength; he often said: "One must write fu before one becomes a true man of letters.
idiomatic: Shou held that Wen Zisheng never wrote a fu at all, and though Xing had one or two, they were not his strength; he often said, "Only when you can write fu do you count as a great man of letters.

literal: He claims only memorials, tables, stele, and epitaphs; everything else is child's play beside that.
idiomatic: He rates himself only on memorials, tables, steles, and epitaphs; all else is child's play.

literal: From the second year of Wuding onward, the state's great affairs, edicts, and military documents were all Shou's work.
idiomatic: From the second year of Wuding on, every great edict and military dispatch of state was Shou's.

literal: Whenever there was urgent alarm he received the order and finished on the spot; sometimes palace envoys pressed him—under his brush it was as if composed overnight. In swiftness of hand Xing and Wen could not match him; in deliberating ritual he was Xing's equal.
idiomatic: When crisis struck he took orders and finished at once; sometimes palace envoys hurried him, yet his brush moved as if the piece had been drafted overnight—swiftness Xing and Wen could not match, while in ritual deliberation he stood even with Xing.

literal: Because Shou's sons and nephews were young he admonished them sternly and wrote the "Pillow Book"; its text runs:
idiomatic: His sons and nephews still young, Shou warned them sternly and wrote the Pillow Book, which reads:

literal: I once read Master Guan's book, which says: "Of what is heavy, nothing weighs like the body; of roads to fear, none like the mouth; of deadlines far off, none like the years.
idiomatic: I once read Master Guan's book, which says, "Of burdens none is heavier than the body; of roads none more fearful than the mouth; of distant deadlines none longer than the years.

literal: To carry the heavy burden along the fearful road toward the distant deadline—only the gentleman can reach it.
idiomatic: To bear that weight along that fearful road toward that far deadline—only a gentleman can arrive.

literal: Pondering it afterward, I sigh long.
idiomatic: Turning it over afterward, I sigh at length.

literal: As a peak stands upright in its mass, yet bears what is hidden beneath without toppling;
idiomatic: A peak rises in its mass, yet bears what lies hidden beneath without toppling;

literal: as mountains hoard their solidity, yet hurry forward under their load and do not stop;
idiomatic: mountains hoard their solidity, yet press on under their burden without halt;

literal: Liang alone dredged the torrent, yet could walk and sing without trembling;
idiomatic: Liang of the ford dredged alone, yet walked and sang without fear;

literal: Jiao Yuan made the path perilous, yet some climbed its heel without alarm;
idiomatic: Jiao Yuan made the cliff road perilous, yet men climbed heel to heel unafraid;

literal: when the nine terraces gather, he rises swift in a blink;
idiomatic: when the nine terraces gather, he lifts swift as a glance;

literal: when the five eras are to be fixed, he seems to ascend remote above.
idiomatic: when the five eras are to be fixed, he seems to climb far above.

literal: If bearing weight has its measure, then the more one bears the firmer it grows;
idiomatic: If the burden has its measure, the more you bear the firmer you stand;

literal: if crossing danger has its art, then one crosses and fears nothing.
idiomatic: if crossing peril has its method, you cross and do not flinch.

literal: What is distant in deadline yet can be threaded through—when fruit answers, it may be relied on.
idiomatic: What is far in deadline yet can be threaded through—when the fruit answers, it is sure.

literal: Is it that divine principle alone is so? Human affairs are the same.
idiomatic: Is it only divine principle that works so? Human affairs are alike.

literal: Alas!
idiomatic: Alas!

literal: Between heaven and earth one toils in the ground of life and death; appetites assail one, fame and profit tug—fine food arrives unbidden, pearls and jade come though feet have not sought them;
idiomatic: Between heaven and earth we toil on the field of life and death; appetites assault us, fame and gain pull—rich fare arrives unbidden, pearls and jade gather though we never went to fetch them;

literal: then arrogance and extravagance arise in turn, and ruin follows at once.
idiomatic: then pride and excess follow one another, and peril comes swift.

literal: Thus the highest knower and greatest sage, wise in subtle signs and wise in judgment, now go forth, now withdraw, not holding to one constant rule.
idiomatic: Yet the highest knower, the greatest sage—subtle in foresight, clear in judgment—now emerge, now withdraw, never fixed to one rule.

literal: When they unfold they rescue the age and complete its tasks; when they roll up, their voices vanish and their tracks disappear.
idiomatic: Unfolded, they save the age and finish its work; rolled up, voice fades and footprints vanish.

literal: Silks, jade, women, pepper and orchid, pitch pipes and notes—flattery finds no way ahead of them;
idiomatic: Silks, gems, women, spice and song—flattery cannot get ahead of them;

literal: weighing flesh to measure bone, greasing lips and prying tongues—hatred and malice do not stand before them.
idiomatic: weighing flesh, sizing bone, oiling lips, whetting tongues—malice cannot stand before them.

literal: Merit and name share the age of mountains and rivers; will and work match metal and stone in hardness.
idiomatic: Fame and merit last with mountains and rivers; resolve and deed match metal and stone in hardness.

literal: This is the thick beam that does not warp, the wandering blade that cuts clean.
idiomatic: Such is the thick beam that does not warp, the blade that finds its gap.

literal: When virtue is not constant, the gold and jade within are lost.
idiomatic: When virtue wavers, the gold and jade within are lost.

literal: They gallop through the human world and stir the drifting vulgar.
idiomatic: They race through the human world and stir the drifting crowd.

literal: They hug the sun's heat and call it cold, pack ravines and gullies and still find it not enough.
idiomatic: They clutch the sun's warmth and call it cold, fill ravines and gullies and still are not satisfied.

literal: The source not clear and the stream runs muddy; the surface not straight and the shadow bends.
idiomatic: Source unclear, stream muddied; face not square, shadow crooked.

literal: Alas!
idiomatic: Alas!

literal: Glue and lacquer—how can they hold firm? Cold and heat press close.
idiomatic: Glue and lacquer—how can they endure? Cold and heat crowd close.

literal: Profit turns to harm, glory turns to shame.
idiomatic: Gain reverses into harm, splendor into shame.

literal: Joy and grief come in turn; getting and losing follow without pause.
idiomatic: Joy and grief alternate; gain and loss follow without end.

literal: Some guard the body yet are seized by demons; souls sink into the prison pit.
idiomatic: Some guard the body yet are seized by demons; souls sink into the pit of law.

literal: Is it that strength of foot is not enough? They are lost because they stand in the game.
idiomatic: Is it that the legs are weak? They are lost because they stand in the match.

literal: Who can say the cart warned of tipping forward, yet the man's teacher woke first?
idiomatic: Who can say the cart warned of a forward fall while the driver's teacher woke first?

literal: I have heard that gentlemen, men of the elegant Way, roam through the classics and feast on letters and history.
idiomatic: I have heard of gentlemen, men of the elegant Way, who roam the classics and feast on letters and history.

literal: The brush has a strange edge; discourse has winning reason.
idiomatic: Their brush holds a keen edge; their talk holds winning reason.

literal: When filial piety and brotherly duty reach their utmost, the spirits connect.
idiomatic: Filial piety and brotherliness at their utmost—and the spirits respond.

literal: They weigh the Way and then walk; they measure the road and then stop.
idiomatic: They weigh the Way, then walk; measure the road, then stop.

literal: From self to things, they put others before themselves.
idiomatic: From self to things, they put others first.

literal: Feeling is not tied to glory or decline; the heart does not stick in anger or joy.
idiomatic: Feeling is not bound to rise or fall; the heart does not stick in anger or joy.

literal: They do not nurture hope in hill and ravine, nor wait for price in the market city.
idiomatic: They do not nurse ambition in hill and dell, nor wait for a price in the market.

literal: Word and act look back at each other; they are careful at the end as at the start.
idiomatic: Word and deed watch each other; they guard the end as the beginning.

literal: Where one of these is present, he stands as a feathered standard.
idiomatic: Where one of these stands, he becomes a feathered standard.

literal: Respectful in station, broad in service—what he knows, he does not leave undone.
idiomatic: Respectful in his post, broad in his service—what he knows, he does.

literal: Whether left or right, the eminent man fits the place;
idiomatic: Left or right, the eminent man suits the post;

literal: without regret, without stinginess—thus high yet not in peril.
idiomatic: without regret, without grudging—high yet not in peril.

literal: Unlike the brave who advance and forget retreat, who clutch gain and fear loss, who stake a fortune of a thousand gold, who chase a salary of ten thousand bushels, who throw themselves at gates of violent wind and hurry into rooms of blazing fire—some trip and fall from their feast, others crouch and lose their firm good fortune.
idiomatic: Unlike the bold who advance and forget retreat, who clutch gain and dread loss, who stake a fortune in gold, who chase a stipend of ten thousand bushels, who hurl themselves through gates of violent wind into chambers of flame—some stumble from the feast they meant to keep, others crouch and forfeit their steady fortune.

literal: Can one not fear?
idiomatic: Can one not fear?

literal: Can one not take warning?
idiomatic: Can one not take warning?

literal: At the gate disaster leans; affairs cannot but be kept secret.
idiomatic: At the gate calamity waits; affairs cannot but be kept close.

literal: Behind the wall an ambush hides; words cannot be let slip.
idiomatic: Behind the wall foes lie in wait; words cannot be let slip.

literal: Examine your words; straighten your conduct.
idiomatic: Scrutinize what you say; square what you do.

literal: Words not good, conduct not straight—the ghost seizes the bully, men bind him in the courtyard path.
idiomatic: Words not good, conduct not straight—the ghost seizes the bully, men bind him in the open court.

literal: In darkness his soul is taken; in daylight his life is cut short.
idiomatic: In darkness his soul is taken; in daylight his life is cut short.

literal: Do not submit to what is not law; do not walk what is not the Way.
idiomatic: Do not bow to what is not law; do not walk what is not the Way.

literal: The public tripod is trust for the self; private jade is not treasure for the person.
idiomatic: The public tripod is trust for oneself; private jade is no personal treasure.

literal: Pass the black dye and it turns indigo; cross the blue and it becomes green.
idiomatic: Pass through the black dye and turn indigo; cross the blue and become green.

literal: Hold the cord and see what is straight; set the water and see what is level.
idiomatic: Hold the cord and see what is straight; set the water and see what is level.

literal: Take only when the time is right—not as good as having no desire.
idiomatic: Take only when the time is right—better still to want nothing.

literal: Know where to stop, know what is enough, and you may escape disgrace.
idiomatic: Know where to stop and what is enough, and you may escape shame.

literal: Therefore in acting one must examine the subtle; in lifting one must be careful at the small.
idiomatic: Therefore in acting one must read the subtle; in raising anything one must guard the small.

literal: Knowing the subtle and thinking ahead, perishing then becomes rare.
idiomatic: Read the subtle and think ahead, and ruin grows rare.

literal: Having examined and being careful, fortune and rank return to you.
idiomatic: Having examined and being careful, fortune and rank gather to you.

literal: In old times Qu Yuan recognized forty-nine faults; Yan Hui for almost three months did not stray.
idiomatic: Of old Qu Yuan marked forty-nine faults; Yan Hui for nearly three months did not stray.

literal: Half-steps without cease reach a thousand li.
idiomatic: Half-steps without cease reach a thousand li.

literal: Overturn one basketful and advance, and you reach ten thousand ren.
idiomatic: Overturn one basketful and advance, and you reach ten thousand ren.

literal: Thus it is said: to go far, start near; to climb high, begin low—great and lasting, moving with the age.
idiomatic: Thus they say: go far from what is near; climb high from what is low—great, lasting, moving with the age.

literal: The moon full as a compass—after that night it wanes.
idiomatic: The moon full as a compass—after that night it wanes.

literal: The hibiscus glorious on the branch—by evening it withers.
idiomatic: The hibiscus blooms on the branch—by evening it withers.

literal: What profit that is not loss? What loss that does not harm?
idiomatic: What gain that is not loss? What loss that does not harm?

literal: Gain should not be many; profit should not be large.
idiomatic: Gain should not be many; profit should not be large.

literal: Only he who dwells in virtue fears its height; only he who embodies truth fears its breadth.
idiomatic: Only he who dwells in virtue fears its height; only he who embodies truth fears its breadth.

literal: When the Way is honored, slanders gather; when the burden is heavy, many hatreds meet.
idiomatic: When the Way is honored, slanders gather; when the burden is heavy, many hatreds meet.

literal: In his success Confucius was harried; in his loyalty the Duke of Zhou was hard pressed.
idiomatic: In success Confucius was harried; in loyalty the Duke of Zhou was hard pressed.

literal: Do not say others are narrow toward me—if I cannot bear it, I cannot cover it.
idiomatic: Do not say others are narrow toward me—if I cannot bear it, I cannot cover it.

literal: Do not say others are generous toward me—if I cannot bear it, I cannot blame them.
idiomatic: Do not say others are generous toward me—if I cannot bear it, I cannot blame them.

literal: Like a mountain's mass, nothing is not held;
idiomatic: Like a mountain's mass, nothing is not held;

literal: like the valley's hollow, nothing is not received;
idiomatic: like the valley's hollow, nothing is not received;
